analysis.one_liner: Shield employers' internal safety audit records from disclosure in workplace safety enforcement.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have kept employers' self-audit records out of OSHA enforcement cases, died in a House subcommittee in the 106th Congress and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Employers sometimes hire outside experts to audit their own factories and job sites for safety hazards. This bill would amend the Occupational Safety and Health Act so those audit records could generally not be demanded by the Labor Department when it inspects, investigates, or enforces the law, except in criminal cases, fatality investigations, or narrow circumstances where the government can first prove a violation using other evidence. The stated idea is to encourage companies to find and fix hazards without fear their findings will be used against them in enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers subject to OSHA rules. Companies that discover hazards through their own audits could keep those findings out of inspections and enforcement proceedings, making it harder for the Labor Department to prove violations or seek penalties based on what the company itself documented.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers facing OSHA inspections and penalties

how_it_helps.text: The bill exempts safety and health audit records prepared by or for an employer from disclosure in OSHA inspections, investigations, and enforcement proceedings, unless the employer volunteers them [S3].

The only required disclosures are for criminal proceedings, fatality investigations, or to establish the cause of an alleged violation where the Labor Secretary first proves the noncompliance with evidence independent of the audit itself [S3].

Even when audit records are disclosed, they are admissible as evidence in civil or administrative proceedings only if the Secretary shows the employer did not act in good faith toward the audit, meaning it did not undertake an appropriate process of abating the hazards found [S3].
Sponsor Rep. Ballenger introduced the bill on April 15, 1999, joined by Reps. Hall of Texas and Stenholm [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Workers, if the bill passed. Records a company generated showing known hazards could be withheld from enforcement, making it harder for the government to prove violations and hold employers accountable for workplace conditions.

drawbacks.text: The bill would remove a key evidence source from OSHA enforcement: a company's own documented knowledge of hazards. Where a hazard injured workers but no independent evidence of noncompliance existed outside the audit, the violation could go unproven [S3].

The disclosure exceptions are narrow. Outside criminal cases and fatality investigations, the Secretary must independently establish noncompliance before even seeing the audit records, and any disclosed records are admissible only if the employer is shown to have acted in bad faith toward the audit [S3] — a burden that could make audits a safe harbor for documented hazards.

Supporters of OSHA's existing rules would argue that shielding self-audits weakens the deterrent effect of the law: a company that finds and logs a hazard faces less risk of penalty if it chooses not to fix it under the bill's flexible 'phased schedule of actions' definition of good faith [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated benefit — more companies auditing themselves for hazards — rests on the assumption that fear of enforcement keeps companies from auditing at all. The cost falls on workers: hazards a company knew about through its own audit could be kept out of enforcement, and the 'good faith' standard, which only requires some process toward abatement such as a phased schedule, could excuse documented hazards that remain uncorrected for long periods. The evidence rules tilt heavily toward the employer, since the burden of proving both independent noncompliance and bad faith falls on the Labor Secretary.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee sent it to a subcommittee, which held a hearing, and no further action was ever taken — it never reached the full House for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Cass Ballenger introduced H.R. 1438 on April 15, 1999, with Reps. Hall of Texas and Stenholm as original cosponsors [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce and, a week later, to its Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, which held a hearing [S5].
It attracted 5 cosponsors — 3 Republicans and 2 Democrats — and received no further action after the subcommittee hearing [S4].
The full House never considered the bill, and it expired at the end of the 106th Congress in January 2001 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers and OSHA enforcement are better off, since no shield for employer self-audit records was enacted. Employers did not gain the protection, but the bill's death was by inaction rather than rejection, so the underlying dispute could return in later Congresses.

sides.party_line_note: There was no floor vote to measure partisanship; sponsorship was nominally bipartisan (the Republican sponsor plus 3 Republican and 2 Democratic cosponsors), but the bill died quietly in committee without opposition ever being recorded.

industries.industry: Employers subject to OSHA regulation (manufacturing, construction, and other regulated workplaces)
industries.note: The bill would have given employers a privilege to keep their own hazard-audit findings out of government inspections and enforcement, raising the burden on OSHA to prove violations with other evidence. Workers in those workplaces would bear the safety consequences. The bill died, so employers gained nothing.

The bill aimed to promote third-party safety audits by protecting their confidentiality, which could have expanded demand for audit services. That benefit depended entirely on enactment, which never happened.
